video_notes.title: Stanford CME295 Transformers & LLMs | Autumn 2025 | Lecture 1 - Transformer
video_notes.contributed: Builds the transformer from first principles: tokenization tradeoffs, Word2vec proxy tasks, why RNNs/LSTMs fail on long-range dependencies, and the self-attention/Q-K-V mechanics with a full worked translation example.

video_notes.title: Stanford CME295 Transformers & LLMs | Autumn 2025 | Lecture 4 - LLM Training
video_notes.contributed: Covers pre-training mechanics and scale (data/compute/cost orders of magnitude, Chinchilla scaling), the distributed-training toolkit (data/model parallelism, ZeRO, flash attention, mixed precision/quantization), and the start of SFT plus evaluation pitfalls and LoRA/QLoRA.

video_notes.title: Stanford CME295 Transformers & LLMs | Autumn 2025 | Lecture 5 - LLM tuning
video_notes.contributed: Walks through preference tuning end to end: collecting pairwise preference data, the Bradley-Terry reward model, RLHF/PPO mechanics (advantage, KL penalty, reward hacking), best-of-n, and DPO as a supervised alternative with its PPO-vs-DPO tradeoffs.

claims.claim: The transformer architecture that underlies today's LLMs comes from a single 2017 paper, after earlier NLP work (word embeddings, LSTMs) had been limited by lack of internet-scale data and compute.
claims.quote: we had the transformers, which were part of a paper that was published in 2017

claims.claim: Tokenization is cutting text into arbitrary units (tokens) before a model can process it, and the choice of unit (character/word/subword) is the first design decision in any text pipeline.
claims.quote: cutting the text with respect to some arbitrary unit of text

claims.claim: Subword tokenizers share roots across related words (bear/bears) so embeddings generalize, at the cost of longer sequences, which is the standard middle ground between word- and character-level tokenization.
claims.quote: leveraging roots of words in order to find what

claims.claim: Word-level tokenizers carry the highest risk of out-of-vocabulary (OOV) tokens at inference time; subword lowers that risk and character-level eliminates it, at the cost of sequence length.
claims.quote: this thing is called OOV, Out Of Vocabulary

claims.claim: Target vocabulary size is on the order of tens of thousands of tokens for a single language, scaling to hundreds of thousands for multilingual/code-covering models.
claims.quote: tens of thousands for one language, hundreds of

claims.claim: Word2vec (2013) proved embeddings could be learned via a proxy task (predict next/surrounding word) and produced interpretable analogies like king:queen::Paris:France.
claims.quote: king is to queen, what this is to that

claims.claim: Typical word/token embedding dimensions are in the hundreds (e.g., 768 is a commonly cited example), far smaller than the vocabulary size used to index them.
claims.quote: 768, for instance, is one example of dimension

claims.claim: RNNs process tokens one at a time while keeping a hidden state that summarizes the sentence so far, which is how they incorporate word order that bag-of-embeddings approaches lose.
claims.quote: keep a hidden representation of the sentence so far

claims.claim: LSTMs extend RNNs with a separate 'cell state' meant to retain information judged important to remember, on top of the regular hidden state.
claims.quote: Long Short-Term Memory

claims.claim: Back-propagating through time in RNNs/LSTMs multiplies many quantities together; when those are below 1 the gradient shrinks toward zero (vanishing gradient), crippling long-range memory.
claims.quote: if it's less than 1, it's vanishing

claims.claim: Attention mechanisms (direct links between a prediction and earlier tokens) were introduced in 2014 specifically to fix RNN long-range dependency problems, three years before the Transformer paper.
claims.quote: it was introduced in 2014

claims.claim: The 2017 transformer paper's title signals its core bet: drop sequential RNN processing entirely and let every token directly attend to every other token at once (self-attention).
claims.quote: named Attention is All You Need

claims.claim: Self-attention gives the same word (e.g., 'bank') a different vector representation depending on context, because representations are computed as a function of all other tokens in the sequence at once.
claims.quote: representation of teddy bear that would be unique to the

claims.claim: Self-attention expresses a token in terms of all others using the query/key/value framework: compare the query to every key for similarity, then take a weighted sum of the corresponding values.
claims.quote: query," "key," and "value," Q, K and V

claims.theme: Attention as matrix math for GPUs
claims.claim: Expressing self-attention in Q/K/V matrix form lets the whole-sequence computation run as matrix multiplications, which is exactly the operation GPUs are optimized for.
claims.quote: GPUs love matrices

claims.claim: The original transformer is an encoder (processes source text) plus a decoder (generates target text) architecture, designed around a translation use case.
claims.quote: an encoder, which is on the left side, and a decoder

claims.claim: In cross-attention, the decoder supplies the query while the encoder's output supplies both the keys and values, so the decoder asks 'what from the input matters' at each decoding step.
claims.quote: the keys and values are actually coming from the encoder

claims.claim: The decoder's self-attention layer is masked so it only looks at tokens already decoded, never at tokens to the right that haven't been predicted yet.
claims.quote: it's called masked, because it only looks at the tokens

claims.claim: Because self-attention gives every token a direct link to every other token (no inherent order, unlike an RNN), transformers add explicit position encodings so the model knows token order.
claims.quote: position encodings, which are there to inform on the position

claims.claim: Multi-head attention runs the Q/K/V projection and attention computation multiple times in parallel with different learned projection matrices, giving the model several independent 'views' to learn different token relationships.
claims.quote: allowing your model to learn different projections

claims.claim: Label smoothing replaces a hard one-hot target (probability 1 on the correct next word) with 1-epsilon plus a small epsilon spread over the rest of the vocabulary, since there's rarely only one valid next word — and it was shown to improve BLEU in the original transformer paper.
claims.quote: label smoothing is a technique that tries to

claims.claim: Attention scores are divided by the square root of the key dimension because raw dot products grow with dimensionality, and this scaling keeps softmax well-behaved.
claims.quote: divide by square root of the dimension of keys

claims.theme: Transformer FFN dimension is expansive, not compressive
claims.claim: Unlike Word2vec's bottleneck hidden layer, the transformer's feedforward block uses a hidden dimension bigger than the input/output embedding size, giving the model more degrees of freedom to build richer features.
claims.quote: the hidden layer is of a bigger dimension than input and output

claims.claim: The transformer stacks N identical encoder blocks and N identical decoder blocks; the final encoder layer's output feeds the cross-attention of every decoder block.
claims.quote: a stacked succession of n encoders

claims.claim: LLM training follows the transfer-learning paradigm: a single expensive pre-training stage teaches general language/code understanding, then cheaper tuning stages adapt the model to specific tasks instead of training from scratch each time.
claims.quote: have what we call a pre-training stage

claims.claim: Pre-training trains an LLM to predict the next token over internet-scale text/code data; more than 90% of modern LLMs for this purpose are decoder-only architectures.
claims.quote: most likely a decoder only model in more than 90% of the cases

claims.claim: GPT-3 was trained on 300 billion tokens while Llama 3 was trained on 15 trillion tokens, illustrating the jump in pre-training corpus size across just a few years.
claims.quote: GPT3 was trained on 300 billion tokens

claims.claim: Training a modern LLM requires on the order of 10^25 FLOPs, a quantity that scales roughly with the product of model parameter count and training token count.
claims.quote: training an LLM is on the order of 10

claims.claim: The Chinchilla scaling-law finding is that for a fixed compute budget there is an optimal training-set-to-parameter ratio of about 20 tokens per parameter; by that measure GPT-3 (175B params, 300B tokens) was undertrained.
claims.quote: training set size that's about 20 times the model size

claims.claim: Pre-training a frontier LLM costs a minimum of millions of dollars and can run into the tens or hundreds of millions, plus a real ecological cost that labs now track.
claims.quote: it can even cost tens of millions of dollars

claims.claim: A pre-trained base model's knowledge is bounded by its 'knowledge cutoff date' — the point at which its training data was collected — and injecting new knowledge afterward without degrading other capabilities is an unsolved, hard problem.
claims.quote: this date is called the knowledge cutoff date

claims.claim: Training requires storing activations (forward pass), gradients (backward pass), and optimizer moments (e.g. Adam's first/second moments) in GPU memory simultaneously, and activation memory scales with model size, batch size, and context length (self-attention is O(n^2)).
claims.quote: activations which are basically the values at each layer

claims.claim: Data parallelism splits a training batch across GPUs, each holding a full model copy, trading extra inter-GPU communication cost (gradient averaging) for reduced per-GPU batch-size memory pressure.
claims.quote: distributes data across GPUs

claims.claim: ZeRO (stages 1-3) removes the redundancy of every GPU storing identical optimizer states, gradients, and parameters by sharding them across GPUs — at the cost of more communication overhead.
claims.quote: zero redundancy optimization

claims.claim: Beyond data parallelism, model parallelism includes expert parallelism (one MoE expert per device), tensor parallelism (splitting big matrix multiplications), and pipeline parallelism (different GPUs own different layer ranges).
claims.quote: expert parallelism techniques

claims.theme: Flash attention origin and memory hierarchy
claims.claim: Flash attention, developed at Stanford in 2022, speeds up attention by exploiting the GPU's two memory tiers: large-but-slow HBM (tens of GB) and small-but-fast SRAM (tens of MB, ~10x faster).
claims.quote: flash attention. It was actually developed here at Stanford

claims.claim: Flash attention's core trick ('tiling') computes softmax exactly on small blocks sent to SRAM end-to-end, avoiding the standard approach's repeated read/writes of large intermediate matrices to slow HBM.
claims.quote: The method is called tiling

claims.theme: Flash attention recomputation wins on both axes
claims.claim: Flash attention recomputes activations during the backward pass instead of storing them, which unusually saves both memory and runtime simultaneously — reported as close to a 10x reduction in HBM reads/writes.
claims.quote: it's like almost a 10x reduction

claims.claim: Quantization lowers numeric precision (e.g., FP32 to FP16) to roughly halve memory footprint and roughly double compute throughput on a GPU, at some cost to numeric granularity.
claims.quote: it takes basically half the memory

claims.claim: Mixed precision training keeps the master weights in FP32 but runs forward/backward pass computations in FP16, because weight updates need high precision to avoid accumulating error while activations can tolerate lower precision.
claims.quote: mixed precision training

claims.claim: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) takes the pre-trained model and further trains it on input-output pairs so it predicts the right tokens for a given input, rather than just continuing arbitrary text.
claims.quote: SFT is uh short for supervised fine-tuning

claims.claim: During SFT the loss is computed only on the output tokens, not the input/instruction tokens — the model is conditioned on the input rather than trained to reproduce it.
claims.quote: we don't put a loss over the input

claims.claim: Instruction tuning is the specific SFT subcategory that turns a raw pre-trained model into a helpful assistant that follows instructions, as opposed to SFT used for narrow task specialization.
claims.quote: instruction instruction tuning

claims.claim: SFT datasets are orders of magnitude smaller than pre-training corpora: GPT-3 reportedly used about 13k SFT examples and Llama 3 about 10 million, versus hundreds of billions to trillions of pre-training tokens.
claims.quote: about 13k used by GPT3 and uh 10 million for lama 3

claims.theme: Pre-trained base model lacks assistant behavior
claims.claim: A base (pre-trained only) model asked a helpful question like 'can I put my teddy bear in the washer?' tends to continue the text pattern (e.g. generate a related but unhelpful sentence) rather than actually answer helpfully, because it has only learned next-token prediction, not assistant behavior.
claims.quote: it has been trained on next token prediction not being an assistant

claims.claim: General capability is commonly reported via MMLU (massive multitask language understanding, ~50+ tasks); reasoning/math via benchmarks like GSM8K.
claims.quote: massive multitask language understanding

claims.claim: Comparing models on a benchmark is unreliable unless both were equally exposed to the benchmark's 'test task' domain during training — a documented phenomenon ('training on the test task') that can inflate scores without real capability gains.
claims.quote: training on the test task not the test set the test task

claims.claim: LMSYS Chatbot Arena ranks models via crowd-sourced pairwise human preference, but it is noisy for new entrants and has been shown to be riggable — e.g. a model can be fingerprinted by asking 'who are you' and the ranking manipulated.
claims.quote: it's easily possible to rig such a leaderboard

claims.claim: 'Alignment' in this course's terminology specifically means the combination of fine-tuning (SFT) plus preference tuning, which together follow pre-training; a newer 'mid-training' stage (same objective as pre-training but on a task-aligned data mix) is also emerging between the two.
claims.quote: fine-tuning and preference tuning um which is which comes after pre-training is what we call alignment

claims.claim: LoRA freezes the pre-trained weight matrix W0 and instead trains two small low-rank matrices (A, B) whose product is added to it, where the rank r is typically very small (up to ~10) relative to W0's dimensions (hundreds/thousands), drastically cutting trainable parameters.
claims.quote: the rank of these matrices which is typically taken very small

claims.claim: Although LoRA's original paper applied low-rank adapters only to attention matrices, later analysis found the feedforward blocks give most of the performance benefit, so modern practice applies LoRA to both.
claims.quote: the feed forward blocks are actually those where putting Lora is most beneficial

claims.claim: LoRA fine-tuning empirically needs about a 10x higher learning rate than full fine-tuning, and performs worse with larger batch sizes — attributed (without firm theory) to the low effective rank and different training dynamics of low-rank matrix products.
claims.quote: you want to use a higher learning rates

claims.claim: QLoRA quantizes the frozen base weights into the NF4 format (quantile-based buckets assuming normally distributed weights) plus double-quantizes the quantization constants, yielding about 16x VRAM savings while training LoRA matrices A/B in bf16.
claims.quote: this method generated 16x

claims.theme: Preference pairs capture tone, not new facts
claims.claim: Preference tuning is built from preference pairs — a rejected model output paired with a preferred rewrite for the same prompt — and is aimed at tone/behavior alignment, not teaching new facts.
claims.quote: this pair would be what what we call a preference pair

claims.claim: Pairwise comparison ('which response is better') is the dominant way to collect human preference data because pointwise scoring is hard to calibrate and listwise ranking is more complex than needed.
claims.quote: pair-wise preference data

claims.claim: RLHF (reinforcement learning from human feedback) is a two-stage process: first train a reward model to score outputs, then use reinforcement learning to update the policy (LLM) toward higher rewards.
claims.quote: RHF stands for reinforcement learning from human feedback

claims.claim: Reward models are trained using the Bradley-Terry formulation: P(y_i better than y_j) = sigmoid(R(y_i) - R(y_j)), fit on pairwise winner/loser data with a negative log-likelihood (cross-entropy-like) loss.
claims.quote: the Bradley Terry formulation

claims.theme: Reward model is pointwise at inference despite pairwise training
claims.claim: Although the reward model is trained on pairwise comparisons, the resulting model scores a single (prompt, response) at inference time with one number — it does not need a pair to make a prediction.
claims.quote: you're training in a pair wise way, but at the end of the day

claims.theme: RL objective balances reward and drift
claims.claim: The RL stage optimizes for higher reward while penalizing divergence (via KL) from the SFT reference model, to avoid catastrophic forgetting, overfitting to a noisy reward model, and training instability.
claims.quote: optimize for higher rewards but then without going too far

claims.claim: Reward hacking is when a policy over-optimizes an imperfect reward proxy (e.g., clapping volume as a proxy for an informative lecture) and maximizes the metric without achieving the real goal.
claims.quote: reward hacking

claims.claim: PPO (proximal policy optimization) is named for keeping policy updates 'proximal' (close) to the previous iteration, using a clipped objective so updates aren't too large in either direction.
claims.quote: PO stands for proximal policy optimization

claims.theme: Advantage and value function via GAE
claims.claim: PPO maximizes 'advantage' (how much better an output is than expected), estimated token-by-token with a jointly trained value function; the standard method is generalized advantage estimation (GAE).
claims.quote: generalized advantage estimation

claims.claim: A full PPO/RLHF setup requires keeping four models resident: the policy being trained, the frozen reference/old-policy model, the reward model, and the value function — a major operational cost versus simpler methods.
claims.quote: you need a lot of models

claims.claim: GRPO, introduced in DeepSeek's math-reasoning paper (DeepSeekMath), is called out as a newer, popular RL algorithm for reasoning models that reduces the need for some of PPO's auxiliary models.
claims.quote: GRPO in the context of reasoning models

claims.claim: RL-based tuning (PPO) is 'on-policy': the model generates its own completions each iteration and is updated based on how good those self-generated outputs are, unlike SFT which trains on fixed, not-self-generated data.
claims.quote: on policy training refers to training that involves the model generating

claims.claim: Best-of-N sampling skips RL training entirely: generate N completions from the frozen SFT model, score each with the reward model, and return the highest-scoring one — but this pushes cost to inference time since you pay for N generations per request.
claims.quote: best of n or bun

claims.theme: Best-of-N latency tax even with infinite compute
claims.claim: Even with unlimited parallel compute, best-of-N still waits for the slowest of N generations to finish, and the expected maximum of N latency samples skews later than a single generation's latency — so it is never free, only trades cost for latency.
claims.quote: you still have to wait more than you would have on a single pass

claims.claim: DPO (direct preference optimization) replaces RLHF's two-stage reward-model-then-RL pipeline with a single loss function optimized directly on preference pairs, requiring no explicit reward model at all.
claims.quote: direct preference optimization

claims.claim: DPO needs only two models in memory — the policy being trained and the frozen reference (SFT) model — compared to PPO's four (policy, old/reference, reward model, value function).
claims.quote: instead of four models you just need two

claims.claim: Benchmark studies cited in the lecture show PPO generally outperforms DPO in final quality, but DPO is far simpler to implement and tune; DPO's weakness is a distribution-shift issue since it doesn't correct for what the model actually tends to generate at inference time.
claims.quote: overall PO performs better than DPO

claims.theme: Choosing PPO vs DPO in practice
claims.claim: The practical choice between PPO and DPO comes down to compute/expertise budget: DPO gets you most of the way with much less tuning effort, while PPO demands RL expertise to babysit training but yields the best achievable results.
claims.quote: PO like the RL bar is very hard to tune right

claims.claim: DPO's paper is titled 'Your Language Model is Secretly a Reward Model' because the implicit reward term in its derivation resolves to a function of the policy itself — no separate reward model is ever needed.
claims.quote: your language model is secretly a reward model

disagreements.topic: Whether PPO's extra complexity is worth it versus DPO

positions.position: Cited benchmarking work shows PPO outperforms DPO overall, implying the RLHF pipeline's complexity pays off in final quality.

The same lecture frames DPO as 'your friend' for most practitioners since it gets close to PPO's results with much less tuning/compute burden, reserving PPO for teams with RL expertise chasing the last bit of performance.

gaps: The lecture explicitly skips the sinusoidal position-encoding formula ('we're not going to dig into that today'), so a reader gets the concept but not the math.
The generalized advantage estimation (GAE) formula itself is described as 'beyond the scope of this class' — the corpus names the technique and paper but not the derivation.
No video in this cluster gives concrete wall-clock or dollar costs for the RLHF/PPO stage specifically (only pre-training costs are quantified).
GRPO is named as the lecture-six topic but not explained in this cluster — readers interested in reasoning-model RL get only a pointer, not a mechanism.
Chinchilla's claim that 'architecture change does not play a big role' in scaling is asserted from the paper but not independently examined or challenged in these talks.
Zero-point and absmax quantization techniques are named as pointers ('stay tuned') but never explained within this cluster.

No discussion of how modern production transformers deviate from the original 2017 encoder-decoder design (e.g., RoPE, grouped-query attention) — this cluster covers the original architecture and training pipeline, not current architectural variants.
